The premium for imported cathode has remained flat in the past two weeks, with trading volumes light. Traders seem to be in a wait-and-see mood for now, as two significant events for the Chinese market will take place this month; namely the annual premium talks between Codelco and Chinese buyers, and China’s transition of power which started on 8th November and will last a week. We have yet to receive any updated news from the premium talks, and market sentiment has not recovered from the recent falls in prices. Most market participants in China are still pessimistic about future conditions, as demand for cathode may slow further with temperatures falling in northern China. However, countering this we would expect to see a seasonal uptick in demand for those semis used in the manufacture of products such as consumer electronics and children’s toys, as export demand increases in the run up to Christmas. The premium for imported ER cathode remains flat in the range of $30-60/t, and the premiums for SXEW cathode remain unchanged at between $30-40/t. We have not recently heard of any changes in cathode stocks levels in Shanghai bonded warehouses. The SHMET spot market price slipped to RMB56,050/t on 9th November, down from RMB57,050/t at the time of our last update on 26th October. The spot price has tracked falls in futures prices as global commodities markets have fallen on renewed worries about the U.S. fiscal cliff, following President Obama’s re-election. rts suggest that Chinese smelters are in discussions to export copper under annual contracts for the first time and that the volume might reach 200,000-400,000t. Exporting is now an option open to the Chinese smelters to expand sales volumes, after the government slashed the 3% export tax in July for those engaged in tolling business. However, we have some doubts about the smelters’ ability to find long-term customers with adequate volume requirements, given that the market is already controlled by major overseas smelters. Additionally, the price gap between the SHFE price + domestic cathode premium and the LME price + external premium is an important consideration for the Chinese smelters, since the differential fluctuates regularly, meaning that exports may not always offer better value than domestic sales. Sources at two major smelters confirmed with us that they are seeking overseas long-term customers in Taiwan, South Korea, South East Asia and the Middle East, as selling through exporting currently allows them to realise better prices. These smelters claim that while cathode produced from domestic mines can be sold at a profit, cathode produced from imported copper concentrate can incur losses, so selling cathode to the export market would be a way to minimise losses. Meanwhile, it is said that not all the smelters who are qualified for tolling are exporting now, because some of them have not yet registered with the Chinese government. (Smelters given a tolling quota include--Anhui Tongling Nonferrous, Jiangxi Copper, Hubei Daye Nonferrous, Yunnan Copper, Gansu Jinchuan Group Co., Ltd, Shandong Yanggu Xiangguang Copper and Baiyin Non-Ferrous Metals Group.) After attending this week’s cable conference in Dongguan City, Guangdong Province, and having conversations with local producers, CRU found the mood to be pessimistic. Most producers expect their 2012 sales volumes to fall by 10-15% y-o-y, due to weak export demand, as we estimate that between 90-95% of their output is used in goods exported to the U.S, Europe, Japan and Brazil. Dongguan lies in the manufacturing belt between Hong Kong and Guangzhou, and is traditionally heavily populated by small to medium-sized enterprises engaged in manufacturing for export

.  The output of local cable producers in Dongguan, who predominantly manufacture thin cables used in electronic equipment, 

amounts to around 10% of China’s total cable market share.  Operating rates of cable producers in Dongguan are said to be around 70-80% currently, which is the same as last year’s level.  However, their raw material stocks (copper rod) have decreased.  Copper rod stocks at major cable producers in Dongguan are between 1-2 days, compared with 4-5 days last year, and small sized producers don’t even hold stocks, they buy rod only when they get orders. 

It is interesting to note that there are 3,000-4,000 small-sized cable producers in Dongguan alone, compared to a total of 10,000 in the whole country.  With such a small market share, relative to the whole country, we see that in the next ten years consolidation in this industry will be inevitable.  We expect that at least 30% of the cable producers could disappear from the industry map as they close or are absorbed by stronger producers. 

We note that most of the other major cable producing regions are less exposed to external economic problems:  Yixing City, Suzhou City in Jiangsu Province, is a major cable-producing location where power cables are mainly produced, as well as Wuwei City in Anhui Province and Ningjin county in Hebei Province.  These regions differ from Dongguan in that their focus is on the internal market as well as exports, and so their trading conditions are far more positive than in Dongguan. 

# SRB reportedly to stockpile cathode 

Media reports this week suggest that the State Reserves Bureau might stockpile non-ferrous metals produced by domestic smelters, including around 400,000 t of aluminium ingots and 165,000 t of copper cathode, primarily in order to support prices.  While intervention in the aluminium market sounds plausible, in CRU’s view it is difficult to see why the copper market, at current price levels, would require such support.  Copper smelters have not performed as badly in terms of profitability as aluminium smelters, and at current price levels we believe Chinese copper smelters are above their breakeven point.

It is also worth noting that the price of copper in its recent range is much high than the last time the SRB intervened in the copper market back in Q1 2009 when prices were at US$3500/t. 

# Market sentiment to be warmed by the party event 

On 8<sup>th</sup> November, China started the seven-day 18<sup>th</sup> National Congress of the Communist Party of China, which is seen as a milestone in stabilising the political situation in China.  The market will keep watch for signs of more government stimulus, but in reality these are longer-term considerations.  In the short term, we expect nothing more than a warming-up in sentiment as a result of the confirmation that power was transferred smoothly.  Although outgoing Presi

dent Hu Jintao announced on the first day of this conference that China aims to double its GDP by 2020 from levels in 2010, we think that big stimulus policies are unlikely at the current time, as the inflation risks do not allow the new Chinese government to pursue a large fiscal easing or to loosen monetary policy; the Chinese government has been very focused on controlling inflation to ensure stability, with economic growth rates a secondary concern.  In addition, since the incoming premier (in charge of the economy) Li Keqiang is seen as a close political ally of current president Hu Jintao, and policy setting in China is thought to follow a form of collective leadership (including retired leaders), a drastic change to economic policy so early into the new administration is unlikely.  That said, some small-sized policies such as tax cuts, rebates to specific industries such as automobile and home appliances might be possible from the new administration.
